slides.title: Creatinine
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Blood (serum) and/or urine  ·  Units: mg/dL, µmol/L

What it is used for: Used to check kidney health, help diagnose kidney disease, monitor known kidney problems and how treatment is working, and check for side effects of medicines that may affect the kidneys. Blood creatinine may be measured alone or within a basic (BMP) or comprehensive (CMP) metabolic panel.

eGFR calculated from blood creatinine reflects kidney health more accurately than creatinine alone. Creatinine clearance (comparing blood and urine creatinine) is less accurate than eGFR but may help in people with very high muscle mass or loss of muscle mass (age, illness, limb loss).

slides.title: Creatinine
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Urine creatinine is used to calculate the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR). Comparing blood creatinine with BUN measured in the same panel can help find the cause of a kidney problem.

NIDDK suggests that laboratories report eGFR whenever serum creatinine is measured. To reduce rounding errors in eGFR equations, creatinine is rounded to two decimal places in mg/dL or to the nearest whole number in µmol/L.

Physiology: Creatinine is a normal waste product made when muscles are used and some muscle tissue breaks down. The kidneys filter it from blood into urine; if the kidneys are not working well, creatinine can build up in blood and less may appear in urine.

slides.title: Creatinine
bullets: High: Possible kidney-related causes of high blood creatinine: kidney disease or injury (including infection, poor blood flow to the kidneys, a blockage in the urinary system or kidney failure) and conditions that affect the kidneys, such as heart failure or diabetes.

High: High creatinine does not always mean a kidney problem: dehydration, muscle disorders and injuries, muscular dystrophy, intense exercise or a diet high in meat can raise it. Certain health problems in pregnancy can also increase creatinine.

slides.title: Creatinine
bullets: Low: Low blood creatinine is uncommon. Possible causes include malnutrition, conditions that make muscles smaller (a long illness, a nerve disorder, muscle loss from aging) and serious liver disease.

slides.title: Creatinine
bullets: Pre-analytics: The person may be asked not to eat meat for 24 hours before the test, because meat can temporarily raise creatinine. If creatinine is part of a BMP or CMP, fasting for up to 12 hours may be needed.
Urine creatinine may require collecting all urine over 24 hours, because creatinine levels vary through the day. During collection the container is kept in a refrigerator or a cooler with ice.
Interferences: Certain medicines and supplements can affect the result, so everything the person takes should be reported.

slides.title: Creatinine
bullets: Limitations: Creatinine alone is not the best way to assess kidney function, because creatinine production depends on muscle mass, diet, age and activity. Its results are therefore often used in calculations or compared with other substances.

A normal creatinine does not rule out kidney disease: it may stay in the normal range in early disease and rise as the disease becomes more serious. A single high result cannot diagnose a specific condition; retesting and/or other tests are usually needed.

slides.title: Urea
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: BUN is often part of a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) and helps diagnose or monitor kidney diseases. Because early kidney disease usually has no signs or symptoms, it is also used to screen people at risk.
BUN is often interpreted together with blood creatinine from the same panel (one of the test’s other names is BUN-to-creatinine ratio); this comparison can help find the cause of a kidney problem.

slides.title: Urea
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: MedlinePlus covers this analyte as the BUN (blood urea nitrogen) test, which measures the amount of urea nitrogen in the blood. Urea nitrogen is a waste product formed as the body breaks down proteins; it is carried in blood and removed by the kidneys in urine.

slides.title: Urea
bullets: High: A high BUN generally suggests that the kidneys are not working well. Other possible causes include dehydration, burns, certain medicines, a high-protein diet and a recent heart attack.
Low: Possible causes of a low BUN include a lack of protein in the diet, malnutrition and liver disease.

slides.title: Urea
bullets: Pre-analytics: Usually no special preparation is needed. If other tests are ordered on the same blood sample, fasting for several hours may be required.
Limitations: BUN levels vary with sex and usually increase with age. An abnormal result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.
BUN is only one measure of kidney function. If kidney disease is suspected, other tests may be needed, such as creatinine and GFR, which estimates how well the kidneys filter blood.

slides.title: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (calculated value)  ·  Units: mL/min/1.73 m²

What it is used for: eGFR is used to screen for kidney disease in people without symptoms, help diagnose it in people with symptoms, find out how serious it is, monitor people treated for chronic kidney disease or taking medicines that could harm the kidneys, and check kidney health before treatments that could affect the kidneys.
NIDDK names eGFR and urine albumin as the two key markers of chronic kidney disease. The same two tests are used to monitor known kidney disease.

slides.title: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: Physiology: The kidneys contain tiny filters (glomeruli) that remove waste and extra water from blood. eGFR usually starts from blood creatinine, but creatinine alone cannot determine eGFR because people make different amounts depending on size, diet and activity, so an equation combines it with personal data such as age and sex.

eGFR can also be calculated from cystatin C, a protein made by many cells whose level is not affected by muscle size, age or diet. NIDDK states that using both creatinine and cystatin C is preferred and more accurate than creatinine alone, especially when eGFR is near a critical decision value such as drug dosing or kidney transplant evaluation.

slides.title: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Measured GFR (mGFR) involves injecting a filtration marker and monitoring how quickly the kidneys clear it from blood. It is complicated and not widely available, so it is usually done only in special situations, such as extreme obesity or before donating a kidney.

slides.title: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · Reference values and decision limits
rows: People tested for kidney disease (NIDDK) — Less than 60 (60 or more is described as the normal range).
People tested for kidney disease (NIDDK) — 15 or less.

slides.title: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
bullets: Low: If the kidneys filter waste too slowly (low eGFR), it may be a sign of damage from kidney disease. An eGFR lower than normal for the person may lead to further tests: urine protein, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, BUN, and kidney ultrasound or CT.

slides.title: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Preparation follows the provider’s instructions: fasting or avoiding certain foods such as meat for several hours may be required, because meat can affect the eGFR result. Certain medicines can also affect results, so all medicines should be reported.

Interferences: eGFR is not reliable with rapidly changing creatinine, extremes of muscle mass and body size, or altered diet patterns. MedlinePlus also lists severe malnutrition, muscle-wasting conditions, advanced liver disease and limb amputation; in such cases a measured GFR (mGFR) may be used.

slides.title: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
bullets: Limitations: In some cases cystatin C is measured instead of creatinine: in people younger than 18 or over 65, with a lot of muscle mass, with obesity, or during pregnancy.
eGFR is an estimate, not a precise measure: it may not always reflect kidney damage, and an abnormal result can occur without damage. Trends in eGFR are therefore preferred over a single value.

NIDDK supports calculating eGFR with CKD-EPI equations that do not include a race coefficient. When values calculated with different equations are compared, part of the change may come from the equation rather than from kidney function.

slides.title: Uric acid
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Blood or 24-hour urine

What it is used for: A blood test helps diagnose gout (usually together with synovial fluid analysis) and monitors uric acid during chemotherapy or other cancer treatment: when cancer cells are killed quickly they release large amounts of purines, and testing helps catch a rise early.
A urine test helps find out whether high uric acid is causing kidney stones and monitors the risk of kidney stones in people with gout.

slides.title: Uric acid
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Uric acid is a normal waste product formed when the body breaks down purines, which are released from dying cells and found in certain foods and drinks. Normally it dissolves in blood, is filtered by the kidneys and leaves the body in urine.

If the body makes too much uric acid or the kidneys remove too little, it builds up in blood and can form needle-shaped crystals in and around joints (gout). High levels can also cause kidney stones or kidney failure, but not everyone with high levels develops these problems.

slides.title: Uric acid
bullets: High: High blood uric acid may occur when the body makes too much or the kidneys cannot remove enough. Eating many purine-rich foods can also raise it: red and organ meats (liver, kidney), some seafood (shellfish, anchovies, sardines, trout, tuna), all types of alcohol and high-fructose corn syrup in soda and sweets.

High: Conditions that may be related to high blood uric acid include gout, kidney disease or kidney stones, leukemia, multiple myeloma, metastatic cancer, side effects of cancer treatment such as chemotherapy, alcohol use disorder and preeclampsia.

slides.title: Uric acid
bullets: High: High urine uric acid may be related to gout, kidney stones or a high risk of them, leukemia, multiple myeloma or metastatic cancer, obesity, or an inherited genetic condition such as Lesch–Nyhan syndrome.
Low: Low blood uric acid is uncommon and usually does not cause health problems; related conditions are usually diagnosed with other tests.
Low: Low urine uric acid may be related to kidney disease, lead poisoning or alcohol use disorder.

slides.title: Uric acid
bullets: Pre-analytics: The urine test requires collecting all urine for 24 hours: the first void is discarded and its time recorded, then all urine for the next 24 hours goes into the container. During collection the container is kept in a refrigerator or a cooler with ice.

Interferences: Many medicines, including aspirin, can affect uric acid levels in blood and urine, and taking niacin (vitamin B3) can also affect results. All medicines taken should therefore be reported.
Limitations: A high uric acid in blood or urine does not always mean a condition that needs treatment—many people have high levels without health problems. More tests may be needed to find the cause.

slides.title: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR)
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Urine (random, early-morning/timed or 24-hour)  ·  Units: mg/g

What it is used for: Most often used to look for signs of kidney disease in high-risk people without symptoms (diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, family history, age over 50, smoking, obesity) and to monitor diagnosed kidney disease and its treatment. Because diabetes is the most common cause of kidney disease, people with diabetes should be tested every year.

slides.title: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR)
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Albumin is a common blood protein, not a waste product, so very little should pass into urine: healthy kidney filters let through at most a trace (often called microalbumin), whereas damaged kidneys may let larger amounts pass. Abnormal urine albumin may be an early sign of kidney disease.

Creatinine, a waste product of daily muscle wear, is usually excreted by the kidneys at a steady rate. Comparing urine albumin with creatinine therefore shows whether albumin is being lost at an increased rate.

UACR = urine albumin (mg/dL) ÷ urine creatinine (g/dL), expressed in mg/g, which approximates albumin excretion in mg/day. Unlike a dipstick test for albumin, UACR is unaffected by variation in urine concentration.

slides.title: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR)
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · Reference values and decision limits · 1/2
rows: People tested for kidney disease (NIDDK; the quick reference applies it to patients with diabetes) — More than 30 mg/g (30 mg/g or less is described as normal). If albumin is found, the test is usually repeated once or twice to confirm.

slides.title: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR)
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · Reference values and decision limits · 2/2
rows: Patients with diabetes evaluated for kidney disease (NIDDK quick reference) — Older term for urine albumin levels not detected by a dipstick test.
Patients with diabetes evaluated for kidney disease (NIDDK quick reference) — More than 300 mg/g; the source describes the term as “sometimes used”.

slides.title: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR)
bullets: High: Higher or increasing urine albumin usually means more serious kidney disease that is likely to get worse faster, and a higher risk of heart and blood vessel disease. Smaller amounts do not always mean kidney disease.

slides.title: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR)
bullets: Pre-analytics: The sample may be a random (spot) urine, an early-morning or timed urine (first thing in the morning or after 4 hours without urinating), or a 24-hour collection. MedlinePlus calls the 24-hour collection the most accurate way to measure urine albumin, while NIDDK’s diabetes quick reference recommends a spot UACR and says 24-hour and timed specimens are not necessary.

Before the sample, the person may need to avoid intense exercise, which can briefly increase urine albumin, and may be asked not to eat meat for a day because meat can affect the result. Ask the provider whether any medicines or supplements could affect it.

slides.title: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR)
bullets: Interferences: Temporary increases in urine albumin can be caused by exercise, certain medicines, fever and inflammation; inflammatory conditions such as urinary tract infection, gum infection (periodontitis) and hepatitis can also raise it. Results may also be affected by muscle density, diet, age and race.

Limitations: An abnormal result needs confirmation: usually two more tests are done within 3–6 months, and early-stage kidney disease is possible if two of three are abnormal. An eGFR blood test is usually ordered as well.
Albumin should not be confused with prealbumin: prealbumin is a different protein, and a prealbumin test is not part of kidney testing.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Urine (clean-catch sample; 24-hour collection in some cases)

What it is used for: A urinalysis may include a visual check, tests for certain chemicals and a microscopic exam; the chemical part checks substances such as protein, glucose, ketones, bilirubin, urobilinogen and nitrites, and dipstick (test strip) methods can be used. Urinalysis is used to check general health, including the urinary tract and kidneys, and helps diagnose kidney and liver problems.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Urine ketones are used to monitor people more likely to develop high ketone levels, such as those with diabetes, long-lasting vomiting or diarrhea, alcohol use disorder, eating disorders or starvation, certain digestive diseases, a low-carbohydrate (“keto”) diet, prolonged very hard exercise, or pregnancy.

Physiology: Normally urine contains very little protein, because tiny kidney filters stop large protein molecules from passing into urine. High urine protein over time may be the first sign that kidney disease or another condition has damaged these filters, so the test can help find kidney damage early.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: High: High urine protein can be temporary, for example due to strenuous exercise, dehydration, diet, stress or pregnancy, so repeat testing may be needed. Protein that stays high is likely a sign of kidney disease or kidney damage, and more tests are needed to find the cause.

High: Normally urine contains little or no glucose because the kidneys return it to the blood. More glucose than normal may reflect high blood glucose (diabetes is the most common cause) or, rarely, a kidney condition such as renal glycosuria or Fanconi syndrome, in which glucose is removed even when blood glucose is normal. Pregnancy and gestational diabetes are also listed.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: High: Many bacteria that cause urinary tract infections (UTIs) change nitrates, a normal chemical in urine, into nitrites, so nitrites in urine usually mean a UTI.

High: When cells cannot get enough glucose, the body breaks down fat for energy, producing ketones. Some ketones in urine are normal, but high levels may indicate ketoacidosis, most commonly diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a medical emergency that often develops quickly and can be life-threatening.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: High: Bilirubin is normally not found in urine. Its presence (bilirubinuria) may be a sign of liver disease, such as hepatitis or cirrhosis, or of a blockage in the bile ducts; it can be an early sign of liver damage and may appear before symptoms do.

High: Normal urine contains some urobilinogen, which helpful gut bacteria make from bilirubin in bile. A higher-than-normal level may be a sign of hepatitis, cirrhosis, liver damage due to medicines or hemolytic anemia.

Low: Too little or no urobilinogen may be a sign of a blockage in the ducts that carry bile from the liver or gallbladder to the intestines, a blockage of blood flow through the liver, or a problem with liver function.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Because the amount of protein and other substances in urine varies during the day, a 24-hour urine collection may give more complete results.

The sample is usually collected by the clean-catch method: after washing hands and cleaning the genital area, the first few seconds of urine go into the toilet and the rest is collected in the container without touching its inside, so that germs from the skin do not get into the sample. Bleeding hemorrhoids or a menstrual period should be reported before the test.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: Fasting may be required before a urine ketone test or when other urine or blood tests are ordered. Some medicines may need to be stopped, but only on the provider’s instruction; all medicines being taken should be reported.
Urine for routine analysis is examined within 1 hour of collection, and the pH must also be tested within 1 hour. If testing is delayed, keep the sample refrigerated until it is analysed.

What changes when urine stands: per the WHO table, glucose falls within about 2 hours both at room temperature and at 4–8 °C (bacteria consume it), and pH rises as ammonium forms, so the urine turns alkaline. The textbook lists the same changes and stresses falsely low glucose after a delay.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: Urine protein is more stable: the WHO table gives 1 day at room temperature, 7 days at 4–8 °C and 1 month at −20 °C.
Interferences: Certain medicines, vitamin C and eating a large meal may affect urine glucose results.
Certain medicines and supplements can affect urine bilirubin and urobilinogen results, so everything being taken should be reported.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: Bilirubin breaks down in light: the textbook says fresh urine must be shielded from sunlight and fluorescent light, because bilirubin oxidises to biliverdin, which the strip does not detect (false negative). The WHO document likewise requires darkness for serum bilirubin stored over 8 hours; it gives no separate time for urine.
Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) can affect the urine glucose result; the textbook lists it as a substance that lowers strip sensitivity and gives a false-negative result.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: Limitations: Urine glucose testing is less accurate than blood glucose testing, so blood tests are now more commonly used to diagnose and monitor diabetes. A normal urine glucose does not exclude diabetes, because urine glucose can be normal while blood glucose is high, and a urine glucose test alone cannot diagnose any condition.

A negative nitrite test does not exclude infection, because some bacteria do not change nitrates into nitrites; results for white blood cells in urine are also considered. Home UTI test strips may miss an infection, and a urine culture shows how much and what type of bacteria are present.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: Ketone results may be a number or reported as a “small”, “moderate” or “large” amount, and normal results can vary with diet, activity level and other factors.
Urine bilirubin is only one measure of liver health, and a urobilinogen test alone cannot diagnose a specific condition; abnormal results may lead to further tests such as a liver panel.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Urine (clean-catch sample; 24-hour collection in some cases)

What it is used for: The microscopic exam is the part of a urinalysis in which urine is examined under a microscope for certain types of cells, crystals and mucus. It may be part of a routine checkup or be ordered when visual or chemical urine results are abnormal or there are symptoms of a urinary or kidney disorder.

Physiology: Epithelial cells cover body surfaces, including the urinary tract. Three types line the urinary tract: transitional cells, renal (kidney) tubular cells and squamous cells; a small number of certain types in urine is normal.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Urine crystals form in the kidneys when certain minerals clump together with other substances, usually when urine has high levels of those minerals or too much or too little acid. A few small crystals are normal; large amounts of certain types may signal a condition needing treatment, and some crystals can stick together to form kidney stones.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: High: Blood in urine (hematuria) may be visible (gross hematuria) or seen only under a microscope or found by urinalysis (microscopic hematuria). Most causes are not serious, such as certain medicines, intense exercise, sexual activity or menstruation.

High: Sometimes blood in urine signals a more serious problem: infection of the bladder, kidney or prostate; bladder or kidney stones; kidney injury; a viral infection such as hepatitis; cancer of the bladder, kidney or prostate; enlarged prostate (BPH); inflammation of the kidney, urethra or bladder; a blood disorder; polycystic kidney disease; or disorders of the ureters. More tests may be needed to find the cause.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: High: Red or white blood cells in urine may in some cases mean a condition that needs treatment, such as a urinary tract infection, kidney disease or liver disease.

High: Epithelial cells are often reported as “few”, “moderate” or “many”; “few” is typically normal. Moderate or many cells may be a sign of a urinary tract infection, yeast infection, kidney disease, liver disease or certain cancers.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: High: Reports usually state whether crystals are present, their amount and what they are made of. Calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate crystals are the most common cause of kidney stones; large amounts of uric acid and urate crystals may form when metabolic problems such as gout or type 2 diabetes make urine too acidic; repeated urinary tract infections may cause large amounts of struvite crystals.

High: A small or moderate amount of mucus in urine is a normal finding. A large amount may be a sign of a urinary tract infection, a sexually transmitted infection, kidney stones, irritable bowel syndrome or bladder cancer, and more tests may be needed to find out why.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: Pre-analytics: For crystals, a clean-catch sample or a 24-hour collection may be used; the 24-hour test may be more accurate because the amount of crystals varies during the day. During collection the container is stored in a refrigerator or a cooler with ice.
Samples are usually collected by the clean-catch method so that germs from the skin do not get into the sample; following all collection instructions carefully helps make results accurate.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: Examine urine for sediment promptly: the WHO table gives sediment stability of 1–2 hours at room temperature and 1–8 hours at 4–8 °C, and it must not be frozen. The textbook likewise requires microscopy within 1 hour of collection.

Formed elements deteriorate with delay: the WHO table gives erythrocytes about 1 hour at room temperature (longer in concentrated urine), and the 2 days listed for casts apply only to concentrated urine (osmolality >300 mosmol/kg). The textbooks note lysis of red cells, breakdown of casts and partial destruction of cells in alkaline urine.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: Interferences: Some medicines and certain foods, such as beets or rhubarb, can also turn urine red. Blood from bleeding hemorrhoids or a menstrual period can get into the sample and affect results, so these should be reported before the test.

Squamous epithelial cells in urine may mean the sample was contaminated with cells from another part of the body, which can happen if the genital area is not cleaned well enough during clean-catch collection.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: Crystals do not always mean a condition that needs treatment: large amounts of some types may be caused by certain medicines (calcium-based antacids, some antibiotics, diuretics, antiviral medicines), a diet with too much animal protein (fish, shellfish, organ meats) or not drinking enough fluids.
Limitations: An abnormal microscopic finding does not always mean a condition that needs treatment; more tests may be needed before a diagnosis can be made.

Refrigerated urine may contain excess precipitated salts and be unsuitable for microscopy. For microscopy, urine can be preserved with 10% formaldehyde (8–10 drops per 300 ml), but it is then unsuitable for other tests.

slides.title: Chronic kidney disease (CKD)
bullets: Early kidney disease usually has no symptoms — only tests show how the kidneys work. Testing is needed with diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease or a family history of kidney failure; yearly with diabetes. Two key tests are used to diagnose and monitor: blood GFR and urine albumin.

slides.title: Chronic kidney disease (CKD)
rows: Estimates kidney filtration; calculated from creatinine.
Albumin passes into urine when the kidneys are damaged; UACR estimates daily albumin loss.
The basis for estimating GFR; it rises as kidney disease gets worse.

slides.title: Chronic kidney disease (CKD)
rows: Results are tracked over time: a stable GFR may mean treatment is working.
If urine albumin stays the same or goes down, treatment may be working.

slides.title: Chronic kidney disease (CKD)
rows: Kidney disease is possible; the clinician decides when to recheck.
Called kidney failure; most people at this level need dialysis or a kidney transplant.
May be a sign of kidney disease. If albumin is found, the test may be repeated once or twice to confirm.

slides.title: Chronic kidney disease (CKD)
bullets: Urine albumin can rise temporarily with exercise, certain medicines, fever and inflammation.

slides.title: Urinary tract infection (cystitis)
bullets: A bladder infection is diagnosed from the medical history, a physical exam and lab tests. With repeat infections, urinary tract imaging or cystoscopy may be used to find the cause.

slides.title: Urinary tract infection (cystitis)
rows: Checks urine for blood and white blood cells; nitrites usually mean a UTI.
Identifies the bacteria and helps choose an antibiotic; results take a few days.
When a more serious infection (such as a kidney infection) is suspected — blood tests and a check of kidney function.

slides.title: Urinary tract infection (cystitis)
rows: Usually means a UTI: many bacteria change nitrates in urine into nitrites.
Nitrites negative but white cells present
Infection is still possible — some bacteria do not make nitrites; white cells in urine may also mean a UTI.
A bacterial infection is likely; susceptibility testing helps choose an effective antibiotic.

slides.title: Urinary tract infection (cystitis)
bullets: Home test strips can miss an infection. If no bacterial infection is found, antibiotics should not be taken — unneeded use leads to resistance.

slides.title: Kidney stones
bullets: Diagnosis is based on medical and family history, diet, a physical exam, lab and imaging tests. Urine and blood tests also help identify the stone type; CT or x-ray shows its location and size.

slides.title: Kidney stones
rows: Checks urine for blood and stone-forming minerals; white cells and bacteria may point to a urinary tract infection.
In blood — when there are signs of a stone; in urine — to find out whether high uric acid is causing stones.

slides.title: Kidney stones
rows: Blood tests check for high levels of stone-forming minerals.

slides.title: Kidney stones
rows: Blood in urine + sharp back or side pain
Supports suspicion of a stone; CT or x-ray shows its location and size.
Uric acid ↑ in blood or urine
May be linked to kidney stones or a high risk of them.
White cells and bacteria in urine
A urinary tract infection may also be present.

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
rows: G1 ≥90; G2 60–89; G3a 45–59; G3b 30–44; G4 15–29; G5 <15 (if persisting >3 months) mL/min/1.73 m²
slides.footnote: The reference interval varies by laboratory, method and population; the laboratory verifies its own interval (verification).

CV <2.3%; bias <3.7%; calibration traceable to a reference material; enzymatic method preferred %

slides.title: A very muscular person who eats a lot of meat and trains intensely has blood creatinine above the laboratory interval. Which interpretation best fits the source?
options: Non-kidney factors (muscle, diet, intense exercise) may contribute; one result is not a diagnosis, so retesting or other tests such as eGFR are needed.
It points to serious liver disease.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source says creatinine depends on muscle and diet, and intense exercise and a meat-rich diet can raise it.

Basis: MedlinePlus: high creatinine is not always a kidney problem (dehydration, muscle factors, intense exercise, meat-rich diet); a single high result is not a diagnosis.

slides.title: Why does a creatinine within the laboratory interval not rule out kidney disease?
options: In early kidney disease creatinine may stay in the normal range and rise only as the disease becomes more serious.
Creatinine is not removed by the kidneys.
Creatinine is meaningful only in urine, not in blood.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source states exactly this; if kidney disease is suspected, other kidney tests are done.

Basis: MedlinePlus: blood creatinine may stay in the normal range in early kidney disease and rises as it becomes more serious.

slides.title: What does the BUN test actually measure?
options: Total protein in the blood, from which urea nitrogen is formed
Creatinine, a waste product released from muscle and removed by the kidneys
Urea nitrogen, a waste product of protein breakdown removed by the kidneys
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: BUN measures the amount of urea nitrogen in the blood.

Basis: MedlinePlus: the BUN test measures urea nitrogen in blood; urea nitrogen forms when proteins are broken down and is removed by the kidneys.

slides.title: A person who has been drinking very little fluid has a high BUN. Which statement matches the source?
options: A high BUN always means kidney disease, whatever the person’s fluid intake has been.
Dehydration is one possible cause of a high BUN, and an abnormal result does not always mean a condition needing treatment.
Dehydration typically lowers BUN rather than raising it, so this high result must reflect a kidney disease needing treatment.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: dehydration is listed among causes of high BUN; if kidney disease is suspected, other tests may be needed.

Basis: MedlinePlus: dehydration is a possible cause of high BUN; abnormal results don’t always mean a condition needing treatment.

slides.title: Why is eGFR calculated with an equation rather than reading kidney function directly from blood creatinine?
options: People make different amounts of creatinine depending on size, diet and activity, so creatinine is combined with factors such as age and sex.
Creatinine is not filtered by the kidneys.
eGFR is measured directly after injecting a filtration marker.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: per the source, creatinine alone cannot determine eGFR.

Basis: MedlinePlus: creatinine alone can’t determine eGFR because its production depends on size, diet and activity; mGFR uses an injected filtration marker.

slides.title: For a patient with a limb amputation or severe muscle wasting, what approach does the source describe?
options: Creatinine-based eGFR stays fully reliable, because muscle mass does not affect creatinine.
eGFR is dropped and BUN alone is used to judge kidney function.
eGFR may be unreliable; a measured GFR (mGFR) with a filtration marker may be used.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: MedlinePlus lists limb amputation and muscle wasting among situations for mGFR.

Basis: MedlinePlus: in severe malnutrition, muscle wasting, advanced liver disease and amputation, eGFR may be unreliable and mGFR gives a clearer picture.

slides.title: The main morphofunctional unit of the kidney is:
In which disease is "meat-slop" colored urine seen:
Creatinine is:
options: the end product of protein metabolism

slides.title: When does residual nitrogen increase due to urea nitrogen:
options: nephritis, acute and chronic renal failure

slides.title: Why is creatinine determined in blood and urine:
In which cases is azotemia retention observed:
Theory of urine formation?
bullets: 1. Urine is formed in the nephron: filtration in the glomeruli (primary urine – protein-free ultrafiltrate of plasma, ~180 L per day), reabsorption and secretion in the tubules, concentration in the collecting ducts.
2. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the main indicator of kidney function; in practice eGFR is calculated from creatinine (and cystatin C).

3. Proximal tubule: glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate, Na and most of the water are reabsorbed; loop of Henle – concentration gradient via the countercurrent mechanism; distal tubule and collecting ducts – final regulation under aldosterone (Na/K) and ADH (water).

slides.title: Theory of urine formation?
bullets: 4. Laboratory reflection: glucosuria (if filtered glucose exceeds reabsorption capacity), proteinuria (glomerular or tubular damage), urine density/osmolality (concentrating ability).
5. Kidney disease is classified by KDIGO by eGFR (G1–G5) and albuminuria (A1–A3).

slides.title: Examining the physical and chemical properties of urine?
bullets: 1. Physical properties: amount (in adults ~600–2000 mL/day), color (bilirubin, blood, hemoglobin/myoglobin, drugs), clarity (turbidity – salts, leukocytes, bacteria, mucus), odor, relative density (1.002–1.035; urinometer, refractometer or test strip) – renal concentrating ability.

2. Chemical examination – test strips: pH (4.5–8), protein (mainly albumin; alkaline pH – false positive), glucose (when the reabsorption threshold is exceeded), ketones (acetoacetate/acetone, β-hydroxybutyrate is not detected), blood (erythrocytes, hemoglobin, myoglobin – peroxidase activity), leukocyte esterase, nitrites (some bacteria), bilirubin, urobilinogen.

slides.title: Examining the physical and chemical properties of urine?
bullets: 3. Interferences: ascorbate (false negative blood, glucose, nitrite, leukocyte esterase), concentrated or dilute urine, drugs (phenazopyridine).
4. Confirmatory tests: for protein – sulfosalicylic acid (all proteins) and quantitative UPCR/ACR, for blood – microscopy, glucose and ketones in blood.
5. Preanalytics: midstream, morning urine, analysis within 1 hour or storage at 4 °C.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy?
bullets: 1. Preparation: 5–12 mL of well-mixed fresh urine, centrifuged at ~400×g for 5 minutes, resuspended in a standard volume; under a coverslip at low (×100) and high (×400) magnification; phase contrast/staining, polarization for crystals.

2. Organized elements: erythrocytes (normal 0–5/field; dysmorphic erythrocytes and acanthocytes – glomerular source), leukocytes (0–5; many – infection, inflammation), epithelium (squamous, transitional, renal tubular), casts.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy?
bullets: 3. Casts: hyaline (a few are normal; concentrated urine, exertion), erythrocyte (glomerulonephritis, vasculitis), leukocyte (pyelonephritis, interstitial nephritis), granular (tubular damage), waxy (severe CKD), fatty (nephrotic syndrome).
4. Unorganized elements: crystals (oxalates, urates, uric acid, triple phosphates – infection; cystine – cystinuria), bacteria, fungi, trichomonads, sperm.
5. Automated urine particle analyzers (flow cytometry, digital imaging) – screening; abnormal results are confirmed by microscopy; the result is standardized per unit volume (/µL).
